title: Reading the notation CS 146 uses
summary: Read n, 2ⁿ, log n, Σ, n^(log_b a), T(n) and O(g(n)) as sentences, out loud, without stopping.
sourceNote: Lectures 4–7 use all of this without explaining it. CLRS ch. 3 covers it in the appendix voice; this is the plain voice.

blocks.md: Every CS 146 lecture is a conversation in a language you haven't been taught. When Poon writes T(n) = 2T(n/2) + kn he reads it out loud as a sentence — "the time to sort n things is twice the time to sort half as many, plus a linear amount of extra work" — but the slide only shows the symbols. If the symbols aren't sentences to you yet, the lecture is noise, no matter how well he teaches. This chapter turns eight symbols into sentences. It's the whole reason the later chapters will make sense.

You already have the one thing this needs: you can program. Every idea here has a for-loop or a function behind it, and I'll show you that version first, because that's the version your brain already trusts.

blocks.body: exponents: repeated multiplication
the number of times you can halve n
a for-loop that adds
an exponent that happens to be a log (only looks scary)
a function that returns "how many steps"
"grows no faster than g"
proving something for all n by proving it for n+1

blocks.md: - **n** — how big the input is

sections.heading: n — the size of the input

blocks.md: n is always "how many things did you give me." Sort an array of 8 numbers: n = 8. Search a list of a million users: n = 1,000,000. We never care about a specific n; we care about what happens as n grows. That's the mental shift of this entire course: stop asking "how long does this take on my array" and ask "if I double the array, what happens to the time?"
blocks.slide: n is a variable, not a number

blocks.title: Every algorithm is a function of n. The question is always: how does the count of steps change as n grows?

blocks.body: The size of the input. Runtime is always described as a function of n, because the only thing we're allowed to vary is how much data we're given.

sections.heading: Exponents — repeated multiplication (and why 2ⁱ keeps showing up)

blocks.md: 2⁵ means "multiply 2 by itself 5 times": 2·2·2·2·2 = 32. n² means n·n. That's all an exponent is. The reason it's everywhere in this course: **anything that doubles once per step is a power of 2.** One thing that splits in two, then each half splits in two again — after i splits you have 2ⁱ pieces.

blocks.caption: Each row doubles the row above. Row i has 2ⁱ boxes. Merge sort's recursion tree is exactly this picture.

blocks.md: Two rules you'll use constantly, both of which are just counting multiplications. **Multiplying powers adds exponents:** 2³·2² = (2·2·2)·(2·2) = 2⁵. **A power of a power multiplies exponents:** (2³)² = 2³·2³ = 2⁶. And the odd-looking one: **anything to the power 0 is 1**, because "multiply by 2 zero times" leaves you with what you started with, which is 1.

blocks.prompt: After 10 rounds of splitting every piece in two, how many pieces are there? And if you have n pieces, what's n as a power of 2 when n = 64?
blocks.answer: 2¹⁰ = 1024 pieces. 64 = 2⁶ (2·2·2·2·2·2). That second question is a log question in disguise — next section.

sections.heading: log n — how many times can you halve it?

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why it exists** Some algorithms don't look at every element — they throw half away at each step. Binary search on a sorted array of 1,000,000 numbers checks the middle, throws away the wrong half, and repeats. How many steps until one element is left? That count is what log means. It's not a mysterious function; it's a counter of halvings.

frames.caption: Halve it: 1. It took 4 halvings, so log₂ 16 = 4. Check: 2⁴ = 16.

blocks.md: So **log₂ n answers the question "2 to what power gives n?"** — which is the same as "how many halvings from n to 1" and the same as "how many doublings from 1 to n." Those are three phrasings of one fact, and Poon uses all three in Lecture 5: he asks "how many times must we halve our search space" and later "how many times must we double 1 to reach n." Same number.

blocks.title: This loop IS the definition. If you can read this, you can read log.

blocks.md: That last row is the whole reason logs matter: a billion items, thirty steps. An algorithm that's O(log n) barely notices how big the input is. When Poon writes plain "log n" with no little 2, he means log₂ — he says so on Lecture 5 slide 35. Other bases work the same way: log₃ 27 = 3 because 3³ = 27, i.e. "how many times can you cut 27 into thirds."

**Rule 1: log(a/b) = log a − log b.** Dividing inside the log becomes subtracting outside. The one you'll see: log(n/2) = log n − log 2 = log n − 1. Halving n costs exactly one halving. **Rule 2: log(aᵇ) = b·log a.** An exponent inside can hop out front as a multiplier. That's the rule that makes n^(log_b a) readable in the next section.

blocks.answer: 5 (2⁵ = 32). 4 — either compute log₂ 16 directly, or use rule 1: 5 − 1. 4 (3⁴ = 81).

blocks.body: The power you raise b to in order to get n. Equivalently, the number of times you can divide n by b before reaching 1. Plain "log" in this course means log₂.

sections.heading: Σ and 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) — a for-loop that adds

blocks.md: The Greek letter Σ (sigma) is a for-loop with an accumulator. Everything below the Σ is the loop's start, everything above is the end, everything to the right is what gets added each iteration.

blocks.title: Read Σ from the bottom up: start i at 1, stop at n, add i each time.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why this particular sum matters** Insertion sort in the worst case shifts 1 element on the first pass, 2 on the second, 3 on the third, up to n−1. Poon writes that total as 1 + 2 + 3 + … + (n−1) on Lecture 4 slide 13 and then just says "= n²-ish." Here's why that's true, so you never have to take it on faith.

blocks.md: So 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2, and the insertion-sort version 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = (n−1)·n/2 = (n² − n)/2. When n is big, the n² term dominates and the /2 is a constant, so this is "about n²" — which is the honest content of the phrase O(n²). ==This is where O(n²) comes from==: not a rule to memorize, but a staircase you counted.

**Where you'll meet this sum after the exam** Any time work grows with progress. Comparing every pair of n things (users, points, files) is this sum — n(n−1)/2 pairs, which is why 'compare all pairs' code dies on big inputs. Appending n items to a structure that shifts or rewrites what's already there: same staircase. Even the party trick is real: n people all shaking hands is n(n−1)/2 handshakes. When you see nested loops where the inner one runs `i` times, ==your brain should say 'staircase, so about n²/2'== before you've finished reading the code.

blocks.answer: 100·101/2 = 5,050. (Gauss allegedly did this in primary school by pairing 1+100, 2+99, … — same staircase.)

blocks.body: A sum over a range: the index starts at the value under the Σ, ends at the value above, and each term to the right is added. The one identity to memorize: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2.

sections.heading: n^(log_b a) — the scariest-looking thing in the course, decoded

blocks.md: The master method (Lecture 7) compares everything against n^(log_b a). It looks like a typo. It isn't — it's an ordinary exponent whose value happens to be computed by a log. Read it inside-out: first compute the little number log_b a, then raise n to that.

frames.caption: Start with the expression. Don't touch n yet.
Evaluate the exponent alone. It's a log question: 2³ = 8, so log₂ 8 = 3.
Substitute. n^(log₂ 8) is just n³. That's the whole trick.

rows: 3^1.26 ≈ 4 — not a whole number, that's fine
blocks.slide: The ones you'll meet in HW 7 and on the midterm

blocks.md: Where does it come from? In Lecture 7 you'll see it's **the number of leaves in the recursion tree**: a problem that splits into a pieces, each 1/b the size, has depth log_b n and therefore a^(log_b n) leaves, and a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) by log rule 2 from the log section (swap which one is the base — it's a legal move because both are "how many times" counts of the same tree). For now, you only need to be able to compute it.

blocks.prompt: T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n. What is n^(log_b a)?
blocks.answer: a = 9, b = 3. log₃ 9 = 2 (3² = 9). So n². (And n is polynomially smaller than n², which will be master-method case 1 → Θ(n²).)

sections.heading: T(n) — a function that returns "how many steps"

blocks.md: T(n) is a function like any you'd write: input a size n, output the number of steps the algorithm takes on an input that size. T(8) is the steps to sort 8 things. T(n/2) is the steps to sort half as many. 2T(n/2) is the steps to sort two halves. You can read every recurrence in the course by translating each term into that sentence.
blocks.slide: T is a function, not a mystery symbol

blocks.title: This is Lecture 6 slide 7, in words. Practice saying each term.
blocks.body:
T(n)      "the steps to handle n things"
  =  2T(n/2)   "twice the steps to handle half as many"   ← the two recursive calls
  +  kn        "plus k·n more steps"                       ← the merge, a constant per element
T(1) = 1  "one thing takes one step"                       ← the base case, where recursion stops

blocks.md: Why is T defined in terms of itself? Because the algorithm is defined in terms of itself — merge sort calls merge sort. A recurrence is just the runtime version of a recursive function. And exactly like a recursive function, it needs a base case or it never stops; Poon says "in most problems it's safe to assume T(1) = 1."

blocks.body: T(n) = the number of steps on input size n. A recurrence relation is an equation that defines T(n) using T of smaller inputs, plus a base case. Solving it means finding a plain formula (no T on the right side) for how T grows.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why this exists — the problem it solves** Suppose you write a search and your friend writes a different one, and you race them. Yours wins. What did you learn? Almost nothing: maybe your laptop is faster, maybe your test array was tiny, maybe your language's `for` loop compiles tighter. Exact timings are ==contaminated by everything that isn't the algorithm== — the CPU, the language, whether `a[i]` counts as one step or three. The question that actually separates algorithms is: **what happens as the input grows?** Double n — does the time double (linear), quadruple (quadratic), or barely move (logarithmic)? That *shape of growth* is the algorithm's own property; it survives every hardware and language change. Big-O is nothing more than a notation for the shape with the contaminated details thrown away on purpose. !!It deliberately cannot tell you which of two O(n) programs is faster!! — that's the detail it discards to say something machine-independent.
blocks.slide: Why we don't count exact steps

blocks.md: **When you actually reach for it** Three moments, and they'll repeat for your whole career. **Before writing code**: choosing — 'contacts are sorted, so binary search O(log n) instead of scanning O(n)'; 'this needs lookups by key, so a hash map O(1) instead of a list walk O(n)'. **After writing code**: explaining — a code review that says =="this is O(n²) in cart size; it dies at 10k items"== ends an argument that 'it felt fast on my machine' never will. **Predicting**: your endpoint handles 1,000 users today; will it survive 100,000? If it's O(n) you buy one bigger box; if it's O(n²) ##no box exists## — you rewrite. Interviews are just this three-way skill compressed into 45 minutes: every LeetCode 'Time Limit Exceeded' is the grader telling you your shape is wrong, not your code.

blocks.title: Same million items, different shapes (at 100M steps/second)
blocks.slide: Why the shape is the whole ballgame

blocks.md: **Where the definition comes from** — it isn't handed down; it's built from the two things we agreed to ignore. We want 'f grows no faster than g' to be a claim about *shape*, so it must survive two attacks. Attack 1: 'my computer runs every step 3× slower, so your f just tripled.' Fine — the definition allows a constant multiplier: we only demand ==f(n) ≤ c·g(n)== for *some* fixed c, and a 3× slowdown just means a bigger c. Attack 2: 'for n = 2 your f is actually bigger than g.' Also fine — small inputs are noise, everything is fast at n = 5. So the definition only promises things ==past some starting line n₀==. Put both allowances into one sentence and you get Poon's Lecture 4 slide 15 definition, exactly: **f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.** Read it as: *once n is big enough, f never rises above some fixed multiple of g.* The c and the n₀ aren't decoration — they ARE the two agreed blind spots, written as math.

Finding a Big-O proof (like 5n + 10 = O(n) below) is literally naming a c and an n₀ that make this picture true.

blocks.title: Poon's proof pattern, step by step
blocks.body:
Show 5n + 10 = O(n). That means: find a c and an n₀ so that 5n + 10 ≤ c·n whenever n ≥ n₀.

1. Guess a c bigger than the leading coefficient. The 5n needs at least 5; pick c = 6 to leave room for the +10.
2. Write the inequality with that c: 5n + 10 ≤ 6n.
3. Simplify: subtract 5n from both sides → 10 ≤ n.
4. That's true whenever n ≥ 10. So n₀ = 10, c = 6, and the definition is satisfied. Done — 5n + 10 = O(n).

blocks.md: In practice nobody hunts for c and n₀ except on an exam question that asks for them. Day to day, you simplify by throwing away what the definition lets you ignore. **Drop lower-order terms** (n² + 100n + 500 → n²: for big n the n² dwarfs the rest). **Drop constants** (the +500). **Drop coefficients** (2n² → n²: that's the c). Poon's slide 23 is exactly these three moves.

**One misconception to kill early** !!Big-O does not mean 'worst case'!! — they're independent ideas that usually travel together. O/Ω/Θ describe a *bound direction* (ceiling / floor / tight); worst/best/average describe *which input* you're measuring. You can put a ceiling on the best case ('even the best case is O(n) — it must read the input') or a floor on the worst case. The reason people conflate them: the most USEFUL sentence in practice is 'a ceiling on the worst case' — ==no input, ever, exceeds this== — so that's the pairing everyone says out loud. When Poon asks for insertion sort's cases: best is Ω(n) (already sorted), worst is O(n²) (reversed) — two different inputs, two different bounds.
blocks.slide: O is a ceiling, not 'the worst case'

rows: grows at least as fast as g
tight — when floor and ceiling match

blocks.prompt: Simplify 3n³ + 40n² + 7 to Big-O. Then: is 2n + 1 = O(n)? Find c and n₀.
blocks.answer: O(n³) — drop 40n² and 7 (lower order), drop the 3 (coefficient). Yes: c = 3 gives 2n + 1 ≤ 3n ⟺ 1 ≤ n, so n₀ = 1. (Lecture 4 slide 16.)

blocks.body: There exist constants c > 0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. In words: past some point, f is bounded above by a constant multiple of g.

sections.heading: Induction — proving something for every n

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why it exists** You can't test a claim for every n — there are infinitely many. Induction is the trick that proves a claim for all n with two finite steps: show it for the smallest case, and show that *if* it holds for one value, it must hold for the next. Then it's true for 1, so for 2, so for 3, forever — like dominoes. Poon uses this twice: loop invariants (Lecture 3) and the substitution method (Lecture 6) are both induction wearing different clothes.

blocks.body: show the claim for the first value (n = 1, or j = 1 in a loop). Poon's loop-invariant word for this: *Initialization*.
assume the claim for some n (the *inductive hypothesis*), and use that assumption to prove it for n+1. Poon's word: *Maintenance*.

blocks.md: - Then conclude it holds for all n. Poon's word: *Termination* (for loops, that's where you read off the final answer).
blocks.slide: The two steps (and Poon's names for them)

blocks.title: Prove 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2 for every n ≥ 1
blocks.body:
The staircase picture convinced you; induction proves it.

1. Base case, n = 1: left side is 1; right side is 1·2/2 = 1. ✓
2. Inductive hypothesis: assume 1 + 2 + … + k = k(k+1)/2 for some k.
3. Inductive step: then 1 + 2 + … + k + (k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) — I used the assumption for the first k terms.
4. Factor out (k+1): (k+1)·(k/2 + 1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2. That is exactly the formula with n = k+1. ✓
5. So the claim passes from every k to k+1, and it held at 1. It holds for all n.

blocks.md: The only move that ever feels like cheating is step 3: "assume it's true for k." It isn't cheating, because you're not claiming it's true for k — you're proving the *conditional* "if it works for k then it works for k+1." The base case is what turns that conditional into an actual fact for every n. When the substitution method says "assume T(n/2) ≤ c(n/2)log(n/2)" in Lecture 6, that's this same step 3.

blocks.body: To prove P(n) for all n ≥ 1: prove P(1) (base case); prove that P(k) implies P(k+1) (inductive step). Loop invariants and the substitution method are induction.

blocks.md: Read each one aloud as a sentence. If any of them still stalls you, go back to that section — the rest of CS 146 will keep using it.

blocks.answer: "The steps for n things equal three times the steps for half as many things, plus n extra." Three subproblems, each half size, linear combine cost. (Its answer, from Lecture 7: n^(log₂ 3) ≈ n^1.58, since 3 > 2 means the leaves dominate.)

blocks.prompt: Σ from i=0 to log n of 2ⁱ
blocks.answer: "Add up 2ⁱ for i from 0 up to log n": 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n. A doubling series — the total is about 2n, which is why the merge sort *divide* step is O(n) overall (n − 1 divisions, Lecture 5 slide 27).
"f grows exactly like n log n" — bounded above AND below by constant multiples of n·log n. Merge sort is Θ(n log n) in every case.

exercises.title: How many halvings?
exercises.prompt: An array has 1,000,000 elements. Binary search halves it each step until one element is left. About how many steps? Do it without a calculator — you only need to know one power of 2.
hints: You're being asked 'how many times can I halve a million before I hit 1'. That number has a name from this chapter.
People reach for log₁₀ and get 6. Wrong base. Every halving is a division by 2, so it's log₂ — and log₂ 1,000,000 is much bigger than 6.
Find a power of 2 near a million: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 ≈ 1,000. So a million ≈ 1,000 × 1,000 ≈ 2¹⁰ × 2¹⁰ = 2²⁰. The exponent is your answer.
solution: Steps = log₂ 1,000,000 (the number of halvings from n down to 1).
Sanity check the other way: 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 — just over a million. ✓
exercises.why: 'A million items, twenty steps' is the single most useful number in computing. It's why databases index, why sorted data is worth keeping sorted, and why an O(log n) algorithm feels instant no matter how big the input gets. You'll estimate this in your head for the rest of your career.

exercises.title: Count the inner loop
exercises.prompt: How many times does `count++` run, as a formula in n? Then give the Big-O.
hints: Don't try to see it all at once. Ask: when i = 0, how many times does the inner loop run? When i = 1? When i = 2? Write those down.
The common mistake is 'two nested loops, so n × n'. That would be right if the inner loop always ran n times — but it runs i times, and i changes. Add up the actual counts.
You're adding 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n−1). That sum has a closed form from this chapter. Then: which term grows fastest?
solution: For i = 0 the inner loop runs 0 times; i = 1 → 1 time; i = 2 → 2 times; … ; i = n−1 → n−1 times.
Expand: (n² − n)/2 = n²/2 − n/2. The n² term dominates; drop the coefficient ½ and the lower-order n/2.
O(n²). (This is HW 4 Problem 2 and the exact shape of insertion sort's worst case.)
exercises.why: Almost every 'why is my code slow' question in a real job is this exercise in disguise: a loop hiding inside a loop, doing n(n−1)/2 work where n(log n) was possible. Being able to count it — not guess it — is what lets you find the fix.

exercises.title: Write the shape of an induction proof
exercises.prompt: Claim: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ⁿ = 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 for every n ≥ 0. Don't prove it yet — just write the three labelled parts you'd need (base case, inductive hypothesis, inductive step), each as one sentence with the actual numbers or expressions filled in.
hints: The base case is the smallest n the claim mentions. Plug it into both sides and check they match.
People write the inductive step as 'assume it's true for all n' — that assumes the conclusion. You assume it for ONE value, k, and show it for the NEXT one, k+1.
In the step, the left side for k+1 is the left side for k plus one more term. Write 'LHS(k+1) = LHS(k) + 2ᵏ⁺¹', then replace LHS(k) with what the hypothesis says it equals.
solution: Base case (n = 0): left side is 1; right side is 2¹ − 1 = 1. ✓
Inductive hypothesis: assume 1 + 2 + … + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 for some k ≥ 0.
Inductive step: 1 + 2 + … + 2ᵏ + 2ᵏ⁺¹ = (2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1) + 2ᵏ⁺¹ = 2·2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 2ᵏ⁺² − 1, which is the claim for k+1. ✓
Conclusion: true for n = 0, and true for k ⇒ true for k+1, so true for all n ≥ 0.
exercises.why: Loop invariants (Lectures 2–3), recurrence proofs by substitution (Lectures 6–7), and every correctness argument you'll ever write for a recursive function are this same three-part shape. Learn the shape once and you can prove code correct instead of hoping.
